title: Liechtenstein Adopts New Constitution Establishing Constitutional Monarchy
description: Prince Johann II promulgated a new constitution on 5 October 1921 transforming Liechtenstein into a constitutional, hereditary monarchy on a democratic and parliamentary basis. The document established the Landtag (parliament), guaranteed civil liberties, and created the dual sovereignty arrangement between the prince and the people that still defines the principality.

title: Customs Union Treaty Signed with Switzerland
description: Liechtenstein concluded a customs union treaty with Switzerland on 29 March 1923, abolishing the customs border between the two states and integrating Liechtenstein into the Swiss customs and economic territory. The agreement followed the dissolution of the previous customs union with Austria-Hungary after World War I and reoriented the principality decisively westward.

title: Swiss Franc Adopted as Official Currency
description: Following the customs union, Liechtenstein replaced the collapsing Austrian krone with the Swiss franc as legal tender, formally tying its monetary system to Switzerland. The currency union eliminated exchange-rate risk with the principality's main economic partner and provided the monetary stability that would later anchor the financial sector.

title: Spar- und Leihkasse Bank Failure Triggers Financial Crisis
description: The Spar- und Leihkasse fuer das Fuerstentum Liechtenstein collapsed in 1928 after speculative losses, wiping out a substantial share of national savings and forcing the princely family to cover deposits from private funds. The failure produced lasting public mistrust of speculative banking and shaped the conservative regulatory ethos that would govern the future financial centre.

title: Prince Franz Josef II Accedes and Declares Wartime Neutrality
description: Franz Josef II became reigning prince in March 1938, the first sovereign to permanently reside in Vaduz, just weeks before Germany's annexation of Austria placed Nazi forces on Liechtenstein's border. He declared and maintained strict neutrality throughout World War II, refusing to join the German Reich despite intense pressure and a small domestic National Socialist movement.

title: Failed National Socialist Putsch Attempt
description: The pro-Nazi Volksdeutsche Bewegung in Liechtenstein attempted an Anschluss-style putsch on 24 March 1939, hoping to force the principality's incorporation into the German Reich. The coup attempt collapsed within hours after Swiss border guards mobilised and German backing failed to materialise, allowing the principality to preserve its independence.

title: Liechtenstein Grants Asylum to 462 Russian Soldiers
description: At the end of World War II, Liechtenstein refused Soviet repatriation demands and granted asylum to roughly 462 soldiers of the First Russian National Army of the Wehrmacht who had crossed the border, becoming the only Western country to defy Stalin's repatriation demands. The exiles were eventually resettled in Argentina with financial assistance arranged by Vaduz, an act later commemorated by a memorial in Hinterschellenberg.

title: Liechtenstein Joins the International Court of Justice Statute
description: Liechtenstein became a party to the Statute of the International Court of Justice in 1950, marking the principality's first significant accession to the postwar multilateral system. The move signalled a quiet reintegration into international institutions even as Liechtenstein remained outside the United Nations for another four decades.

title: Princely Family Establishes LGT Bank
description: The princely House of Liechtenstein founded Liechtenstein Global Trust (LGT), originally Bank in Liechtenstein, in 1920 but expanded it sharply through the 1950s as a private bank serving European wealth. LGT became the cornerstone of a banking model built on confidentiality, low taxes, and the discreet trust foundation (Stiftung) vehicle that would define the principality's financial centre.

title: Liechtenstein Joins the International Court of Justice as Litigant
description: Liechtenstein filed the Nottebohm Case before the International Court of Justice against Guatemala, producing one of the most cited rulings in international nationality law. Although Liechtenstein lost, the case established the principle of effective nationality and signalled the principality's willingness to use international legal institutions to defend its citizens.

title: Major Rhine Flood Devastates Lowland Communes
description: Severe flooding of the Rhine and its tributaries in autumn 1968 inundated parts of Vaduz, Schaan, and the lowland communes of Liechtenstein, causing widespread property damage. The event accelerated investment in flood defences, river canalisation, and emergency infrastructure that would protect the corridor in subsequent decades.

title: Liechtenstein Joins the European Free Trade Association as Observer
description: Liechtenstein gained observer status in EFTA through its customs union with Switzerland during the 1970s, deepening its integration into European trade arrangements without surrendering sovereignty. The arrangement allowed the principality to benefit from European market access while maintaining its bilateral relationship with Bern.

title: Male-Only Referendum Rejects Female Suffrage
description: Liechtenstein's male electorate narrowly rejected granting women the right to vote in a national referendum in 1971, with similar male-only votes failing again in 1973. The repeated failures isolated Liechtenstein as the last country in Europe to deny women the franchise and drew sustained international criticism.

title: Liechtenstein Joins the Council of Europe
description: Liechtenstein became the twenty-first member of the Council of Europe in November 1978, accepting the European Convention on Human Rights and the supervisory jurisdiction of the European Court of Human Rights. Membership marked the principality's most significant step toward European institutional integration to that date.

title: Female Suffrage Approved by Razor-Thin Margin
description: On 1 July 1984, Liechtenstein's male voters approved female suffrage at the national level by 51.3 percent, making the principality the last country in Europe to grant women the right to vote. Communal-level voting rights were extended in subsequent referendums between 1984 and 1986, completing the long-delayed franchise extension.

title: Hans-Adam II Accedes to the Throne
description: Prince Hans-Adam II became reigning prince on 13 November 1989 following the death of his father Franz Josef II, beginning a reign that would be marked by constitutional reform and a more assertive role for the monarchy. He had effectively governed as regent since 1984 and brought a sharply business-oriented vision to the principality.

title: Liechtenstein Joins the United Nations
description: Liechtenstein became the 160th member of the United Nations on 18 September 1990, ending decades of self-imposed exclusion from the global body and signalling full integration into the postwar multilateral order. Membership coincided with the principality's broader push to assume a more visible international profile.

title: Liechtenstein Joins EFTA as Full Member
description: Liechtenstein became a full member of the European Free Trade Association on 1 September 1991 after Switzerland negotiated a new customs treaty allowing the principality to act independently in trade matters. EFTA membership opened the door to participation in the forthcoming European Economic Area negotiations.

title: Constitutional Crisis over EEA Referendum Date
description: Prince Hans-Adam II clashed publicly with Prime Minister Hans Brunhart in 1992 over scheduling Liechtenstein's referendum on joining the European Economic Area, with the prince threatening to leave the country if his preferred timing was overruled. The dispute exposed unresolved tensions in the dual-sovereignty constitutional model that would later drive the 2003 reform.

title: Liechtenstein Joins the European Economic Area
description: After a 1992 referendum approved accession by 55.8 percent, Liechtenstein joined the European Economic Area on 1 May 1995, gaining access to the EU single market without becoming an EU member. EEA membership required harmonising large parts of Liechtenstein's regulatory framework with EU law and reshaped its banking, insurance, and labour rules.

title: Liechtenstein Joins the World Trade Organization
description: Liechtenstein became a founding member of the World Trade Organization in September 1995, completing the principality's accession to the postwar multilateral trade architecture. WTO membership locked in market-access commitments alongside its EEA and EFTA obligations.

title: FATF Blacklists Liechtenstein over Money Laundering
description: The Financial Action Task Force placed Liechtenstein on its list of non-cooperative countries and territories in June 2000, citing weak anti-money-laundering rules and opaque trust foundation structures. The blacklisting triggered an emergency overhaul of the Due Diligence Act and the creation of the Financial Intelligence Unit, removing the principality from the list within a year.

title: Financial Market Authority Created Following FATF Reforms
description: Liechtenstein established the Financial Market Authority (FMA) and the Financial Intelligence Unit in 2001 as part of an emergency response to the FATF blacklisting and growing international pressure on its financial centre. The reforms tightened due diligence, beneficial ownership disclosure, and supervision across banking, insurance, and trust services.

title: Constitutional Referendum Expands Princely Powers
description: On 16 March 2003, voters approved Prince Hans-Adam II's controversial constitutional revision by 64.3 percent, granting the monarch broader powers including dismissal of the government, veto over legislation, and judicial appointments. The reforms were criticised by the Council of Europe's Venice Commission as a step backward for democracy but accepted on the basis that voters retained the right to abolish the monarchy.

title: Hereditary Prince Alois Becomes Regent
description: Prince Hans-Adam II transferred day-to-day exercise of sovereign powers to his son Hereditary Prince Alois on 15 August 2004, making Alois effective head of state while the prince retained the throne. The arrangement was designed to ensure continuity and prepare the next generation for the expanded constitutional powers granted in 2003.

title: LGT Data Theft Scandal Triggers German Tax Investigation
description: In February 2008 German authorities launched a sweeping tax-evasion investigation after the BND paid roughly 4.6 million euros for stolen LGT Treuhand client data, exposing thousands of foreign account holders including high-profile German executives. The scandal devastated Liechtenstein's reputation as a discreet financial centre and forced rapid concessions on banking secrecy and information exchange.

title: Liechtenstein Removed from OECD Grey List
description: Liechtenstein signed multiple tax information exchange agreements during 2009 and adopted OECD standards on transparency, allowing the OECD to remove it from its grey list of uncooperative tax havens later that year. The reforms ended decades of unconditional banking secrecy and reoriented the financial centre toward compliant wealth management.

title: Same-Sex Civil Partnerships Legalised by Referendum
description: Liechtenstein voters approved a registered civil partnership law for same-sex couples by 68.8 percent in a June 2011 referendum, granting most of the legal protections of marriage. The reform marked one of the principality's most progressive social-policy votes despite the population's strong Catholic affiliation.

title: Referendum Rejects Curbing Princely Veto
description: On 1 July 2012, voters rejected by 76 percent a citizens' initiative that would have stripped Prince Hans-Adam II and Hereditary Prince Alois of the right to veto referendum results, after the princely family had threatened to disengage from politics if the proposal passed. The defeat consolidated the monarchy's expanded powers from the 2003 reform.

title: Liechtenstein Joins the Common Reporting Standard
description: Liechtenstein signed up to the OECD's multilateral Common Reporting Standard for automatic exchange of financial-account information in 2014, with first exchanges starting in 2017. The commitment ended what remained of traditional banking secrecy and aligned the principality fully with the global tax transparency regime.

title: FATCA Agreement with the United States Enters into Force
description: Liechtenstein's intergovernmental agreement with the United States under the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act took effect in 2015, requiring Liechtenstein financial institutions to report on US-linked accounts. FATCA implementation completed the principality's transition from secrecy jurisdiction to fully transparent financial centre.

title: Vaduzer Medienhaus Restructuring Reshapes Press Landscape
description: Consolidation of Liechtenstein's two main daily newspapers under restructured ownership during 2017 narrowed the principality's already small media market and prompted public debate about pluralism. The episode highlighted the structural challenges of sustaining diverse independent media in a country of fewer than 40,000 people.

title: Liechtenstein Posts Record GDP per Capita
description: Liechtenstein's GDP per capita exceeded 165,000 US dollars by 2017, ranking among the very highest in the world driven by financial services, precision manufacturing led by Hilti and Ivoclar Vivadent, and a workforce roughly half of which commutes daily from neighbouring Switzerland and Austria. The performance underscored the resilience of the post-secrecy economic model.

title: Blockchain Act Establishes Token and Trustworthy Technology Framework
description: The Landtag passed the Token and Trustworthy Technology Service Providers Act in October 2019, creating one of the world's first comprehensive legal frameworks for tokenisation, crypto-asset custody, and blockchain-based financial services. The law positioned Liechtenstein as a regulated alternative to less-supervised crypto jurisdictions.

title: Archbishop Wolfgang Haas Controversy Resurfaces
description: Long-running tensions between the Archdiocese of Vaduz under conservative Archbishop Wolfgang Haas and the Liechtenstein government peaked in 2019 over religious-education arrangements, church-state separation, and the archdiocese's autonomy. The dispute revived calls to formally separate church and state, building on a 2012 framework agreement that remained partially unimplemented.

title: COVID-19 Pandemic Response and Cross-Border Coordination
description: Liechtenstein recorded its first COVID-19 cases in March 2020 and coordinated its response closely with Switzerland and Austria, including border controls, vaccine procurement through the Swiss programme, and digital contact-tracing. The principality reported relatively low excess mortality but faced disruption to its cross-border workforce, which makes up roughly half of all employees.

title: Liechtenstein Marks Constitution Centenary
description: The principality commemorated the 100th anniversary of its 1921 constitution throughout 2021 with state ceremonies, scholarly conferences, and a programme of public events highlighting a century of constitutional monarchy. The centenary was used by the princely house to underscore institutional continuity amid debates over future succession arrangements.

title: Daniel Risch Becomes Prime Minister
description: Daniel Risch of the Patriotic Union (VU) was sworn in as prime minister on 25 March 2021 following the February general election, leading a continued grand coalition with the Progressive Citizens' Party (FBP). The election left the long-standing two-party system intact but registered modest gains for the populist Democrats for Liechtenstein (DpL).

title: Liechtenstein Implements EU and Swiss Sanctions on Russia
description: Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Liechtenstein adopted EU sanctions packages in line with its EEA obligations and freezing measures coordinated with Switzerland. Implementation tested the principality's financial-sector compliance regime given its role in trust and wealth management for international clients including Russian beneficial owners.

title: Banking Sector Faces Declining Client Base
description: Liechtenstein's banking sector reported continued attrition of European clients during 2023 as automatic information exchange and tightened beneficial-ownership rules eroded the historical secrecy premium, with assets under management increasingly concentrated in non-European wealth. The trend forced consolidation among smaller banks and trust providers.

title: Princely Family Foundation Reform Approved
description: The Landtag approved a package of reforms to Liechtenstein's foundation (Stiftung) law during 2024 tightening transparency, beneficial-ownership reporting, and governance requirements following persistent EU and OECD pressure. The reform marked another step in the principality's incremental shift away from the discreet trust-foundation model that had defined its post-war financial centre.

title: Brigitte Haas Becomes First Female Prime Minister
description: Following the February 2024 general election, Brigitte Haas of the Patriotic Union (VU) was designated to form a government, becoming Liechtenstein's first female prime minister when sworn in in early 2025. The result confirmed the VU's lead and continued the grand-coalition tradition while marking a milestone in a country that had granted women the vote only forty years earlier.

title: Liechtenstein Negotiates Updated EEA-Crypto Framework
description: Liechtenstein continued negotiating implementation of the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation through the EEA framework during 2025, seeking to preserve the early-mover advantage of its 2019 Blockchain Act. The talks tested the limits of regulatory autonomy within the EEA arrangement and the durability of the principality's crypto-finance niche.
